This page helps you get started on your final project: getting your team repository onto your machine, then the
files and tools your team and your assistants work with. What to hand in, and when, is on the
[setup and proposal](project-proposal.qmd) page.

## Getting your team repository

Your team repository is `CPSC436C-2026W-T1/team_NN` on github.students. github.students works only on UBC networks:
on campus, or over the [UBC VPN](https://it.ubc.ca/services/email-voice-internet/myvpn).

1. **Sign in.** Open <https://github.students.cs.ubc.ca> and sign in with your CWL.
2. **Add an SSH key.** In your github.students settings, under SSH keys, add your public key (for example
   `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`). If you do not have one, create it with `ssh-keygen -t ed25519`.
3. **Check the connection.** Run `ssh -T git@github.students.cs.ubc.ca`. It greets you by your CWL.
4. **Clone.** `git clone git@github.students.cs.ubc.ca:CPSC436C-2026W-T1/team_NN.git`, with your team's number.

`main` is protected: every change goes in by pull request, approved by someone other than its author.

## Files in your repository

The pull request "Course files: team rules and templates" brings `AGENTS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`,
`experiments/TEMPLATE.md`, the `docs/` templates for the proposal, requirements, design and tasks, an example
architecture sketch, the resource list `docs/resources.md`, `scripts/teardown.sh`, and the MCP configuration
examples. The spec checker `tools/spec_check.py` arrives with the course files for checkpoint 1, when you write
requirements.

| File | What it is | Where to use it |
|------|------------|-----------------|
| `AGENTS.md` | Project instructions for coding assistants: project name and team, AWS lease and Region, how to use the course MCP, review procedure, pull request rules, and boundaries. | Repo root. Fill in the placeholders once at project start. Assistants read it at the start of every session. |
| `.mcp.json` | MCP server config with the course server `436c` URL. It reads your token from the `KB_MCP_TOKEN` environment variable. Copy it from `.mcp.json.example`. | Repo root, on your machine only. It is in `.gitignore`, so never commit it. |
| `docs/proposal.md` | The seven proposal sections as headings. | Write it for the proposal tag. |
| `docs/requirements.md` | Numbered requirements R010, R020 … in EARS form, each with numbered constraints and a Given/When/Then test, plus assumptions Q010, Q020 …. | Write it after the proposal, before the design and tasks. Cite R ids in design, tasks, pull requests and reviews. |
| `docs/design.md` | The architecture sketch (elements D010, D020 …), the data layout table, correctness properties P010, P020 … that each validate an R line, and the Lens answers table. | Write it after the requirements. Update it through a pull request when the architecture changes. |
| `CONTRIBUTING.md` | How work gets into the repository (issues, branches, checks, pull requests, reviews) and the team agreement: roles, meetings, response times, disagreements. | Repo root. Fill in the placeholders as a team in your first week and merge it through a pull request. |
| `docs/tasks.md` | Build steps S010, S020 …, each naming the R lines it serves and what it measures to show they hold. | Use it to plan and split the work. Name the S ids in each pull request. |

## Getting Started with Kiro

Kiro offers students a free year through
[Kiro for Students](https://kiro.dev/changelog/general/kiro-for-students/), which allows:

- One year of free access to Kiro, both the IDE and the CLI, including spec-driven development.
- 1,000 credits per month for 12 months.
- No credit card and no trial timer.

### How to register

Full instructions: [kiro.dev/students](https://kiro.dev/students/#instructions).

1. **Sign up or log in.** Go to [kiro.dev/students](https://kiro.dev/students/) and sign in with **AWS Builder ID**
   (recommended) or **GitHub**. Google also works. Whichever you choose, the email on that account must be your
   **UBC student email**.
   If you already have a Kiro account, link your UBC email to it.
   - Do **not** use the "Your organization" sign-in option. The student program does not support it.
2. **Verify your student status.** After signing in, open your account usage page. Eligible accounts see a banner that
   says "You are eligible for Kiro Students". Click verify and complete the SheerID check, which takes about a minute.
3. **Start building.** Once you are verified, you get 1,000 credits per month for one year.

Credits do not roll over from month to month, and you cannot buy add-on credits under the student plan. After the
year, your account drops to the Kiro free tier. Your code and specs stay in your repo. For help, use the student
channel on the Kiro Discord.

> After you register, install the Kiro CLI or IDE and sign in with the same account.

## Setting up AGENTS.md

### What AGENTS.md is for

`AGENTS.md` is the instruction file for the coding assistant in your project. Kiro, Copilot CLI and Claude Code
read it when a session starts. Claude Code reads it when the repository has no `CLAUDE.md`, from version 2.1.277; on
an older version, update Claude Code. See [AGENTS.md in the Claude Code docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#agents-md). It tells the assistant what it would otherwise have to guess:

- **What the project is:** the project name, the team, the course, and the AWS lease and Region you work in.
- **Where the design lives:** `docs/requirements.md`, `docs/design.md` and `docs/tasks.md` are the source of truth, and
  the file gives the id rules (R, D, P, S, Q) the assistant must follow when it edits them.
- **Where facts come from:** the assistant searches the course MCP server before it states a number or a rule about
  AWS, Spark or file formats, and uses the AWS Knowledge MCP for AWS documentation.
- **How work is done:** the review procedure, how to run the spec checker, how pull requests are written and
  attributed.
- **What is off limits:** no committed credentials, no public buckets, no `"Action": "*"` or `"Resource": "*"`, and no
  hourly-billed resources or IAM changes without asking a person first.

Think of it as the brief you would give a new teammate on day one. The assistant follows it in every session, so a
wrong or missing value here shows up in everything it produces.

### Instructions

1. **Open `AGENTS.md` in the repo root.** The template ships with placeholders in angle brackets, `<…>`. Fill in
   the placeholders, and adapt the rules to your team. Change a rule only through a pull request the team agrees on.

2. **Fill in the Project line.**

   | Placeholder | What to write | Example |
   |-------------|---------------|---------|
   | `<project name>` | A short name for your system | `TransitLens` |
   | `<one sentence: …>` | What the system does and for whom | `Hourly ridership dashboards for city transit planners` |
   | `<team-id>` | Your team id: `t` and your team number | `t07` for `team_07` |
   | `<names>` | Every team member's name | `Ana Lee, Sam Roy` |

3. **Fill in the AWS line** once your team has its AWS lease. Until then, leave it and fill in the rest.

   | Placeholder | What to write | Example |
   |-------------|---------------|---------|
   | `<team>` (profile) | The AWS CLI profile name for your group lease | `t00` |
   | `<amount>` | The team's budget for the term | `$20` |

   Do **not** add the 12-digit AWS account id anywhere. The assistant gets it from
   `aws sts get-caller-identity` when it needs it. Keep the Region as `ca-central-1`.

4. **Fill in the Working on AWS section.**

   | Placeholder | What to write | Example |
   |-------------|---------------|---------|
   | `<team>` in `aws sso login --profile <team>` | The same profile name as above | `t00` |
   | `<team-id>-` | The name prefix for every resource | `t00-` |
   | `Team=<team-id>, Owner=<name>` | The tags on every resource | `Team=t00, Owner=Ana Lee` |
   | `<date>` (final teardown) | The date every resource must be deleted by | `2026-12-15` |

5. **Check that nothing is left**, apart from the AWS line if your team has no lease yet. Search the file for the
   placeholders:

   ```bash
   grep -n -E "<(project name|one sentence|names|team|team-id|amount|date|name|URL)" AGENTS.md
   ```

6. **Commit through a pull request.** `AGENTS.md` is shared by the whole team. Push the change on a branch and have
   another member approve it; no direct pushes to `main`.

## Setting up CONTRIBUTING.md

`CONTRIBUTING.md` is the same kind of file for the people on the team that `AGENTS.md` is for the assistants. The
repository process and review rules are already written and match `AGENTS.md`. Your team fills in the project name,
the test command, the link to your development guide, the places to ask questions, and every row of the Team
agreement table.

1. **Meet as a team** and go through the rows of the Team agreement table: roles, meetings, response time, working
   style, disagreements, sources, missed commitments. Write a sentence or two for each.
2. **Adapt the rest of the file** to your team, including the `<…>` placeholders: the title, the test command, the development guide link and Where to ask. If
   you have no tests or development guide yet, write "none yet" and fill them in when you build the first slice.
3. **Commit through a pull request** approved by someone other than its author. Every member reads it before it is
   merged.

## MCP Setup

If you use an assistant, connect it to two MCP servers:

- Course MCP Knowledge Base
- AWS Knowledge MCP

You can find both in the `.mcp.json` example.

Set the environment variable for the course MCP server. Your own token is in the issue "Your course MCP tokens" in
your `team_NN` repository. Use only your own, and put this line in your shell profile, not in a file in the repository:

```bash
export KB_MCP_TOKEN=<TOKEN_FROM_INSTRUCTOR>
```

### AI Tool Setup

#### Claude Code Setup

1. Install Claude Code and sign in: [Claude Code quickstart](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/quickstart). Claude Code
   runs on your own Claude account or API key.
2. Copy `.mcp.json.example` to `.mcp.json` in the repo root. Claude Code reads it directly. `.mcp.json` is ignored by
   git, so your token stays on your machine.

Docs: [Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp)

- See *Installing MCP servers → Option 1: Add a remote HTTP server* for `claude mcp add --transport http …`.
- See *MCP installation scopes → Project scope (`.mcp.json`)*. Claude Code reads the project's `.mcp.json` in the repo
  root directly.

#### Kiro CLI Setup

1. Register with [Kiro for Students](#getting-started-with-kiro), then install the Kiro CLI or IDE:
   [Kiro CLI docs](https://kiro.dev/docs/cli/).
2. Copy `.kiro/settings/mcp.json.example` to `.kiro/settings/mcp.json`. It holds the same two servers.

Docs:

- [Kiro CLI: MCP overview](https://kiro.dev/docs/cli/mcp/)
- [Kiro CLI: MCP configuration](https://kiro.dev/docs/cli/mcp/configuration/)

> Kiro does not read `.mcp.json`. It reads `.kiro/settings/mcp.json` in the project, or `~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json`
globally. Add servers with `kiro-cli mcp add` or by editing that file, which uses the same top-level `mcpServers`
object. Remote servers take a `url` and optional `headers`.

### Testing MCP Server Connection & Tools

Your `AGENTS.md` already tells your assistant when to use these sources. To make it more reliable, you could add explicit rules, for example: "If the task involves AWS costs, always check current pricing via the AWS Knowledge MCP server."

Generally, you can specifically ask an agent to use an MCP server and tool in a plain-language prompt. **However, it’s also worth learning how to see which tools an MCP server exposes and how to tell the agent to call them directly.**

#### Claude Code: call a specific MCP tool

You can check if you are connected and what tools are available:

```bash
claude mcp list          # should show aws-knowledge: ✓ Connected
claude                   # then run /mcp to see the tool names
```

Run Claude Code headlessly and approve the AWS Knowledge server's tools in advance:

```bash
claude -p "Use the aws-knowledge aws___search_documentation tool to find S3 bucket naming rules. Cite sources." \
  --allowedTools "mcp__aws-knowledge"
```

- `-p` runs a single prompt non-interactively and prints the response.
- Tools are named `mcp__<server>__<tool>`. `--allowedTools "mcp__aws-knowledge"` approves every tool from this server
  without asking. It does not stop the assistant from trying other tools.
- To allow a single tool, use its full name exactly as `/mcp` shows it, for example `mcp__aws-knowledge__search_documentation`. Some versions of the server add a prefix to tool names, so copy the name rather than guessing it.

#### Kiro CLI: call a specific MCP tool

You can check if you are connected and what tools are available:

```bash
kiro-cli mcp status      # or start kiro-cli and run /mcp or /tools
```

Run Kiro CLI headlessly and approve only the AWS Knowledge search tool:

```bash
kiro-cli chat --no-interactive --require-mcp-startup \
  --trust-tools=@aws-knowledge/aws___search_documentation \
  "Use the aws-knowledge aws___search_documentation tool to find S3 bucket naming rules. Cite sources."
```

- `--no-interactive` runs without a chat session and prints the first response.
- `--trust-tools` approves the listed tools up front. The `@` prefix marks a tool as coming from an MCP server rather than a built-in tool (like `read` or `shell`): `@aws-knowledge/aws___search_documentation` means the `aws___search_documentation` tool from the server named `aws-knowledge` in `mcp.json`. Use `@aws-knowledge` alone to trust all of that server's tools. Run `/tools` in an interactive session to see the exact names.
- `--require-mcp-startup` exits with code 3 if an MCP server fails to start, so a broken setup fails loudly instead of answering from the model's own knowledge.

## Connecting tasks, requirements and the board

Your assistant keeps three things linked: `docs/requirements.md` (the R lines), `docs/tasks.md` (the S rows, each
citing the R lines it serves) and your GitHub Project board. The "Tasks and the project board" section of
`AGENTS.md` holds the rules. For them to work, the assistant needs:

1. **Board link.** Add its URL to `metadata/team.yml` in your course repository, as a line `board: <URL>`. Also put
   it in the "Project board" line of the Project section of `AGENTS.md`, so the assistant finds it in the repository
   it works in.
2. **GitHub CLI with the project scope.** Install [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/) and sign in with `gh auth login`
   on each host you use. The assistant creates issues and board items through `gh`. Add the project scope:
   - github.com: `gh auth refresh -h github.com -s project`;
   - github.students: `gh auth refresh -h github.students.cs.ubc.ca -s project`, on a UBC network.
3. **Permission to run `gh`.** In Kiro CLI, trust the shell tool for the session, for example
   `kiro-cli chat --trust-tools=read,write,shell`. In Claude Code, allow `gh` commands when it asks.

Test it at checkpoint 1, once your requirements and first tasks exist. Add one S row to `docs/tasks.md` with an empty Issue cell, and prompt:

> Read AGENTS.md. Sync docs/tasks.md to the project board.

**It passes when** the assistant creates one issue titled `S010: …` with the label `task`, adds it to the board as
Todo, and opens a pull request that writes the issue number into the row. Run the same prompt again: it should
report that everything is in sync and create nothing.

The assistant never writes R lines to make a check pass. If a task needs an R line that does not exist, it stops and
tells you.

## Setup Testing

You can test if you configured your MCP and `AGENTS.md` correctly by running this test:

1. Start your assistant (Claude Code or Kiro) in the repo folder.
2. Check the status of your MCP servers.
   1. For Kiro CLI, type `/mcp` to see every active server and tools
   2. For Claude Code CLI, use `claude mcp list`. This reports each server as connected, needs authentication, failed to connect, pending approval, rejected through `disabledMcpjsonServers`, or disabled for this project.
3. Give the AI Agent this first prompt within the project root:

   > Read AGENTS.md. Fetch the course start page and tell me what it offers.

4. Watch which tools it calls.

Run it with your own token, never another member's. The course MCP server records each call under your token;
you hand in nothing for it.

**It passes when** the assistant calls `get_kb_doc` on `436c-student/index.md` without you giving it the path, and then
summarizes the course pages the start page lists. The path comes from `AGENTS.md`, so a pass shows that the assistant
read the file and that it can reach the course server.

**If it fails:**

- *It does not call `get_kb_doc` at all:* the course server is not connected. Check that `.mcp.json` (Claude Code) or
  `.kiro/settings/mcp.json` (Kiro) exists, and that your token is set in your shell.
- *It calls the tool but the call errors:* check the server URL and the token. Your token is in the issue "Your course MCP tokens" in your course repository.
- *It asks you for the path, or guesses another one:* it did not read `AGENTS.md`. Check that the file is in the repo
  root and that you started the assistant from that folder.
